## Two Variances {#sec-two-variances}

```{r}
#| label: setup-3-5
#| include: false
source(if (file.exists("R/setup.R")) "R/setup.R" else "../R/setup.R")
funds <- read.csv(data_path("fund_returns.csv"))
fund_A <- funds$return[funds$fund == "A"]
fund_B <- funds$return[funds$fund == "B"]
```

### Learning Objectives

1. Read the $F$ table (Table 7), including lower-tail values from the reciprocal rule.
2. Construct and interpret a confidence interval for the ratio $\sigma_1^2/\sigma_2^2$.
3. Test whether two population variances are equal, by hand and with `var.test()` in R.

### Concept

Is one investment riskier than another? Are prices more stable in one market
than in another? These questions compare two variances. We compare them with a
**ratio**, not a difference:
$$
F = \frac{s_1^2}{s_2^2}.
$$
If the two populations are normal with equal variances, this ratio follows an
**$F$ distribution** with two degrees of freedom: $\text{df}_1 = n_1 - 1$
(numerator) and $\text{df}_2 = n_2 - 1$ (denominator). Like $\chi^2$, the $F$
distribution is positive and skewed to the right.

The $F$ test is also the starting point for the next two topics: Section 3.6
uses it to choose between two $t$ tests, and Chapter 4 (ANOVA) is built on an
$F$ ratio.

### Reading the $F$ Table

Table 7 gives $F$ values with area **0.90, 0.95, 0.975, 0.99 or 0.995** to the
left, one page for each area. Columns are $\text{df}_1$ (numerator) and rows are
$\text{df}_2$ (denominator). The order of the df matters.

Areas such as 0.025 and 0.05 are not printed. Use the **reciprocal rule**, which
swaps the two df:
$$
F_{\alpha,\,\text{df}_1,\,\text{df}_2} = \frac{1}{F_{1-\alpha,\,\text{df}_2,\,\text{df}_1}}
$$

**Example 3.5.1.** Find (a) $F_{0.95,\,4,\,10}$, (b) $F_{0.975,\,12,\,15}$, (c) $F_{0.025,\,12,\,15}$.

::: {.callout-tip icon=false collapse=false}
## Solution

(a) Page for 0.95, column 4, row 10: $F_{0.95,\,4,\,10} = `r crit_F(.95, 4, 10)`$.

(b) Page for 0.975, column 12, row 15: $F_{0.975,\,12,\,15} = `r crit_F(.975, 12, 15)`$.

(c) Swap the df and use the 0.975 page:
$F_{0.025,\,12,\,15} = \dfrac{1}{F_{0.975,\,15,\,12}} = \dfrac{1}{`r crit_F(.975, 15, 12)`} = `r num(crit_F(.025, 12, 15))`$.

```{r}
#| label: fig-f-12-15
#| fig-cap: "Areas 0.025 in each tail of the F distribution with df = (12, 15)"
#| fig-height: 2
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-align: center
crit_plot("F", "two", df1 = 12, df2 = 15)
```
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false}

Find
(a) $F_{0.95,\,3,\,20}$, (b) $F_{0.975,\,8,\,10}$, (c) $F_{0.025,\,8,\,10}$.

```{r}
#| label: curves-3-5-1
#| layout-ncol: 3
#| fig-subcap: ["", "", ""]
#| fig-height: 1.8

blank_curve("F", 3, 20); blank_curve("F", 8, 10); blank_curve("F", 8, 10)
```

::: {.answer title="Your Turn 3.5.1"}
(a) $F_{0.95,\,3,\,20} = `r crit_F(.95, 3, 20)`$

(b) $F_{0.975,\,8,\,10} = `r crit_F(.975, 8, 10)`$

(c) $F_{0.025,\,8,\,10} = 1/F_{0.975,\,10,\,8} = 1/`r crit_F(.975, 10, 8)` = `r num(crit_F(.025, 8, 10))`$
:::

### Formulas and Conditions

**Conditions:** two independent random samples from **normal** populations.

**$(1-\alpha)100\%$ confidence interval for $\sigma_1^2/\sigma_2^2$**
$$
\left(\frac{s_1^2/s_2^2}{F_{1-\alpha/2,\,\text{df}_1,\,\text{df}_2}},\;
      \frac{s_1^2/s_2^2}{F_{\alpha/2,\,\text{df}_1,\,\text{df}_2}}\right)
= \left(\frac{s_1^2/s_2^2}{F_{1-\alpha/2,\,\text{df}_1,\,\text{df}_2}},\;
      \frac{s_1^2}{s_2^2}\,F_{1-\alpha/2,\,\text{df}_2,\,\text{df}_1}\right)
$$
If the interval contains 1, the data are consistent with equal variances.

**Test statistic** for $H_0: \sigma_1^2 = \sigma_2^2$, with df $= (n_1-1,\ n_2-1)$
$$
F_{\text{cal}} = \frac{s_1^2}{s_2^2}
$$

| $H_1$ | Critical region |
|:---:|:---|
| $\sigma_1^2 \ne \sigma_2^2$ | $F_{\text{cal}} < F_{\alpha/2,\,\text{df}_1,\,\text{df}_2}$ or $F_{\text{cal}} > F_{1-\alpha/2,\,\text{df}_1,\,\text{df}_2}$ |
| $\sigma_1^2 < \sigma_2^2$ | $F_{\text{cal}} < F_{\alpha,\,\text{df}_1,\,\text{df}_2}$ |
| $\sigma_1^2 > \sigma_2^2$ | $F_{\text{cal}} > F_{1-\alpha,\,\text{df}_1,\,\text{df}_2}$ |

**In R:** `var.test(x1, x2, alternative = ...)` uses $F = s_1^2/s_2^2$ with `x1` in the numerator.

```{r}
#| label: ex-3-5
nA <- length(fund_A); nB <- length(fund_B)
vA <- round(var(fund_A), 4); vB <- round(var(fund_B), 4)
F_cal <- round(vA / vB, 3)
F_hi <- crit_F(.975, nA - 1, nB - 1); F_hi_swap <- crit_F(.975, nB - 1, nA - 1)
F_lo <- crit_F(.025, nA - 1, nB - 1)
ci_lo <- round(F_cal / F_hi, 4); ci_hi <- round(F_cal * F_hi_swap, 4)
ov <- var.test(fund_A, fund_B)
```

### Example

**Example 3.5.2.** An investor compares the risk of two mutual funds using
their monthly returns (%): `r nA` months for Fund A and `r nB` months for Fund B. The sample variances are $s_A^2$ = `r num(vA)` and
$s_B^2$ = `r num(vB)`. Assume returns are normally distributed.

(a) Construct a 95% confidence interval for $\sigma_A^2/\sigma_B^2$.
(b) At $\alpha$ = 0.05, test whether the two funds have different variances (risk).

::: {.callout-tip icon=false collapse=false}
## Solution

$\text{df}_1 = `r nA` - 1 = `r nA - 1`$, $\text{df}_2 = `r nB` - 1 = `r nB - 1`$,
$s_A^2/s_B^2 = `r num(vA)`/`r num(vB)` = `r fmt(F_cal, 3)`$.

**(a)** $F_{0.975,\,`r nA - 1`,\,`r nB - 1`} = `r F_hi`$ and $F_{0.975,\,`r nB - 1`,\,`r nA - 1`} = `r F_hi_swap`$:
$$
\left(\frac{`r fmt(F_cal, 3)`}{`r F_hi`},\; `r fmt(F_cal, 3)` \times `r F_hi_swap`\right)
= (`r fmt(ci_lo, 4)`,\; `r fmt(ci_hi, 4)`)
$$
We are 95% confident that the ratio $\sigma_A^2/\sigma_B^2$ is between
`r fmt(ci_lo, 4)` and `r fmt(ci_hi, 4)`. The interval does not contain 1.

**(b)**

**Step 1: Hypotheses.** $H_0: \sigma_A^2 = \sigma_B^2$ $\quad H_1: \sigma_A^2 \ne \sigma_B^2$

**Step 2: Level of significance.** $\alpha$ = 0.05

**Step 3: Test statistic.**
$$
F_{\text{cal}} = \frac{s_A^2}{s_B^2} = \frac{`r num(vA)`}{`r num(vB)`} = `r fmt(F_cal, 3)`,
\qquad \text{df} = (`r nA - 1`,\ `r nB - 1`)
$$

**Step 4: p-value.** From the R output below, p-value = `r fmt(ov$p.value, 4)`.
(With the table: critical region $F_{\text{cal}} < `r num(F_lo)`$ or $F_{\text{cal}} > `r F_hi`$.)

**Step 5: Decision and interpretation.** p-value = `r fmt(ov$p.value, 4)` <
$\alpha$ = 0.05, so we reject $H_0$. That is, the variances of the monthly
returns of the two funds are different at the 0.05 level of significance; since
$s_A^2 > s_B^2$, Fund A is riskier.
:::

### Reading R Output

```{r}
#| label: r-data-funds
#| echo: !expr show_code
#| code: !expr c(vec_code("fund_A", fund_A), vec_code("fund_B", fund_B))
```

```{r}
#| label: r-funds
#| echo: !expr show_code
var.test(fund_A, fund_B)
```

| Output | Meaning |
|:---|:---|
| `F = ` | $F_{\text{cal}} = s_1^2/s_2^2$ |
| `num df`, `denom df` | $\text{df}_1 = n_1 - 1$, $\text{df}_2 = n_2 - 1$ |
| `95 percent confidence interval` | CI for $\sigma_1^2/\sigma_2^2$ |
| `ratio of variances` | $s_1^2/s_2^2$ |

R's CI (`r fmt(ov$conf.int[1], 4)`, `r fmt(ov$conf.int[2], 4)`) differs a little from
the hand calculation because R uses unrounded $F$ values.

```{r}
#| label: yt-3-5
yx_n <- 11; yx_s <- 2.8; yy_n <- 21; yy_s <- 1.9
y_F <- round(yx_s^2 / yy_s^2, 3); y_c <- crit_F(.95, yx_n - 1, yy_n - 1)
```

### Your Turn

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Your Turn 3.5.2

An analyst compares the daily price changes (%) of two stocks. For Stock X,
$n$ = `r yx_n` days and $s$ = `r yx_s`; for Stock Y, $n$ = `r yy_n` days and
$s$ = `r yy_s`. Assume normality. At $\alpha$ = 0.05,
test whether Stock X is more volatile (has a larger variance) than Stock Y,
using the critical region from Table 7.
:::

::: {.workspace steps="names"}
:::

::: {.answer title="Your Turn 3.5.2"}
**Step 1.** $H_0: \sigma_X^2 = \sigma_Y^2 \quad H_1: \sigma_X^2 > \sigma_Y^2$

**Step 2.** $\alpha$ = 0.05

**Step 3.** $F_{\text{cal}} = `r yx_s`^2/`r yy_s`^2 = `r num(yx_s^2)`/`r num(yy_s^2)` = `r fmt(y_F, 3)`$, df = (`r yx_n - 1`, `r yy_n - 1`)

**Step 4.** $F_{0.95,\,`r yx_n - 1`,\,`r yy_n - 1`} = `r y_c`$. Critical region: $F_{\text{cal}} > `r y_c`$.

**Step 5.** $F_{\text{cal}} = `r fmt(y_F, 3)`$ does not fall in the critical region
($`r fmt(y_F, 3)` < `r y_c`$), so we accept $H_0$. That is, the variances of the
daily price changes of the two stocks are equal at the 0.05 level of significance.
:::

### Formula Summary

| | Formula |
|:---|:---|
| Conditions | independent samples; both populations normal |
| Reciprocal rule | $F_{\alpha,\,\text{df}_1,\,\text{df}_2} = 1/F_{1-\alpha,\,\text{df}_2,\,\text{df}_1}$ |
| $(1-\alpha)100\%$ CI for $\sigma_1^2/\sigma_2^2$ | $\left(\dfrac{s_1^2/s_2^2}{F_{1-\alpha/2,\,\text{df}_1,\,\text{df}_2}},\ \dfrac{s_1^2}{s_2^2}F_{1-\alpha/2,\,\text{df}_2,\,\text{df}_1}\right)$ |
| Test statistic | $F_{\text{cal}} = s_1^2/s_2^2$, df $= (n_1-1,\ n_2-1)$ |
| R | `var.test(x1, x2, alternative = ...)` |

```{r}
#| label: ex-3-5-exercises
set.seed(2745)
rate_bankA <- round(rnorm(16, 7.2, 0.9), 2)
rate_bankB <- round(rnorm(21, 6.8, 0.5), 2)
eo <- var.test(rate_bankA, rate_bankB, alternative = "greater")
```

### Exercises

**3.5.1** Find (a) $F_{0.99,\,5,\,12}$, (b) $F_{0.05,\,6,\,20}$, (c) $F_{0.975,\,24,\,30}$.

::: {.answer title="Exercise 3.5.1"}
(a) `r crit_F(.99, 5, 12)` (b) $1/F_{0.95,\,20,\,6} = 1/`r crit_F(.95, 20, 6)` = `r num(crit_F(.05, 6, 20))`$ (c) `r crit_F(.975, 24, 30)`
:::

**3.5.2** A regulator compares the interest rates (%) on personal loans from two
groups of lenders: `r length(rate_bankA)` loans from group A and
`r length(rate_bankB)` from group B. It wants to know whether
rates vary more in group A. Use the output to write the decision and
interpretation at $\alpha$ = 0.05.

```{r}
#| label: r-data-banks
#| echo: !expr show_code
#| code: !expr c(vec_code("rate_bankA", rate_bankA), vec_code("rate_bankB", rate_bankB))
```

```{r}
#| label: r-ex-3-5
#| echo: !expr show_code
var.test(rate_bankA, rate_bankB, alternative = "greater")
```

::: {.answer title="Exercise 3.5.2"}
$H_0: \sigma_A^2 = \sigma_B^2 \quad H_1: \sigma_A^2 > \sigma_B^2$.
$F_{\text{cal}} = `r fmt(eo$statistic, 3)`$, df = (`r eo$parameter[1]`, `r eo$parameter[2]`),
p-value = `r fmt(eo$p.value, 4)` < $\alpha$ = 0.05, so we reject $H_0$. That is,
interest rates vary more in group A than in group B at the 0.05 level of significance.
:::
